lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: Eval: grade with Ember by default, keep Spark producer
lines.text: Muse Ember (`muse-ember-1.0`) grades by default because repeated rescore checks put it at parity for less time. It has no contributor variant, so the harness passes `--contributor-mode off` for it; with the mode on it fails with "does not exist or you lack access". Across five runs each on `comprehende-50` and `comprehende-57`, Ember-vs-Spark verdict agreement (median 50 of 52) overlapped Spark-vs-Spark (51 of 52), grader tokens matched at the median, no run failed to parse, and Ember graded about 3.7 times faster. The producer stays on Spark contributor: Ember spot checks wrote thinner reviews, and on the Model API Ember output costs $0.50 per 1M tokens against Spark contributor $0.20 (input $0.10 both; Ember bills the whole request at $0.30 input and $1.50 output over 200K input tokens).

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: File notes: reject lockfile paths, grade file notes as claims
lines.text: Only `validate` and the `case.json` expects (why, parts, groups, size, source kinds, mechanical paths, together, apart) change the exit code. The grader is one read-only call per case. It gets the review, the diff of every group, the frozen sources, and the `Must`, `Good`, and `Must not` lists from `expected.md`. It answers yes or no per item with a quote, and marks each document `lookFor` bullet, group `attention` note, focus caption, line note, and file note the review wrote as true or false at head. The case line shows `must 3/4  good 1/2  mustNot 0/3  bullets 2/2 true`. A false bullet is the costly error: the review told the reader something that is not so.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: Eval: one rubric grader per case, read from expected.md
lines.text: The grader does not judge grouping or prose quality. Grouping is checked by `together` and `apart`. Prose is linted: em dashes, sentences over 25 words, summaries with more sentences than the skill allows, and summaries that read as a path list. Lints print on the case line and in the report and do not fail the case.

lines.summary: Shorter reviews: about 0.74x the words, with file notes and an easy what
lines.text: The case line and the run total print `words`: the prose a review writes for the reader. Titles, summaries, whys, `lookFor`, attentions, questions, captions, notes, file notes, and source gists count. A copied PR comment body does not. Each run also prints `words a->b` per case under `--baseline`.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: Shorter reviews: about 0.74x the words, with file notes and an easy what
lines.text: One run of a skill does not measure it. The same skill scored `must` 30 and 39 in two trials, and CI runs scored higher than local runs of the same skill. Run both skills side by side from the same machine, with `--repeat 3` and `--skill <dir>` for the old one, and compare totals across the trials. A fact a review loses to a tight length costs `must`, so read the lost items before you tighten the skill's usual lengths.

lines.summary: Eval: snapshot the skill per run, add --repeat, --jobs, --skill, --keep
lines.text: - Run the eval in the background with output going to a log file. Arm one wake-up for when the process exits, and do not poll the log or `ps`.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: Eval: snapshot the skill per run, add --repeat, --jobs, --skill, --keep
lines.text: - `pnpm eval` runs `pnpm build` first, and two builds at once race on `dist/`. For parallel streams, run `pnpm build` once, then start `tsx scripts/eval/run.ts --case <id>` per stream. `run.ts` does not build, so after a code change it runs the old `dist/` until you build again. `--jobs <n>` runs n cases in one process instead.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: Eval: snapshot the skill per run, add --repeat, --jobs, --skill, --keep
lines.text: - To stop a run, kill only the processes whose cwd is your checkout, for example `pgrep -f scripts/eval/run.ts` and then `lsof -a -d cwd -p <pid>` for each pid. A broad `pkill` also stops evals in sibling worktrees.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: Eval: snapshot the skill per run, add --repeat, --jobs, --skill, --keep
lines.text: - Clones of case repos are cached in `comprehende-eval-cache/` under `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`, so all worktrees share one cache. A lock lets parallel runs fill it safely. Each case then gets its own clone in the temp dir.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: Eval: use contributor mode for Muse Wonder too
lines.text: Runs use the `muse` CLI login (`muse login`), which spends the subscription, by default — even when `MUSE_CODE_API_KEY` is set. `--use-api-key` spends that key (pay as you go) instead. `--cli-login` names the default and wins over `--use-api-key`. CI writes the repo secret `MUSE_AUTH_JSON` (a CI-only device login, not your daily one) to `~/.config/muse/auth.json` and checks it with `muse usage`; only a missing secret falls back to `--use-api-key` with `MUSE_CODE_API_KEY` — a failed check keeps the subscription so a dead login fails visibly instead of silently spending API credit. Refresh an expired CI login by running `muse login` once in any Linux environment with a fresh `HOME` (a container works), then `gh secret set MUSE_AUTH_JSON < ~/.config/muse/auth.json`. Every Muse run resolves a bare `muse-spark-<version>` id to its `-contributor` tier and passes `--contributor-mode on` for that tier and for `muse-wonder` ids, which Muse Code offers in either mode; other ids, such as `muse-spark-1.3-turbo` and `muse-ember-1.0`, stay unchanged and get `--contributor-mode off`, because they have no contributor variant. The `muse` CLI must be on `PATH`. The eval workflow installs it. Locally, install the CLI the way `.github/workflows/eval.yml` does.
